### What is 'data quality'?

Databases containing biodiversity information - such as those that can be queried using 
galah - contain millions of records supplied by hundreds of organisations, having been 
collected over centuries. It is unsurprising, therefore, that they contain some errors.
In this context, two key questions for users of that data are:

- How large a problem are those errors for their use case? and
- What tools exist to help us solve them?

Data quality systems in galah are built on a set of fields called 'assertions'.
These are usually binary (true/false) variables that flag that something might be wrong 
with the data, generated either programmatically or by users. You can see them by calling 
`show_all_assertions()`:


```
## # A tibble: 126 × 4
##    id                                 description                          category type      
##    <chr>                              <chr>                                <chr>    <chr>     
##  1 AMBIGUOUS_COLLECTION               Ambiguous collection                 Comment  assertions
##  2 AMBIGUOUS_INSTITUTION              Ambiguous institution                Comment  assertions
##  3 assertionUserId                    Identity of user making an assertion Comment  assertions
##  4 BASIS_OF_RECORD_INVALID            Basis of record badly formed         Warning  assertions
##  5 biosecurityIssue                   Biosecurity issue                    Error    assertions
##  6 COLLECTION_MATCH_FUZZY             Collection match fuzzy               Comment  assertions
##  7 COLLECTION_MATCH_NONE              Collection not matched               Comment  assertions
##  8 CONTINENT_COORDINATE_MISMATCH      continent coordinate mismatch        Warning  assertions
##  9 CONTINENT_COUNTRY_MISMATCH         Continent country mismatch           Warning  assertions
## 10 CONTINENT_DERIVED_FROM_COORDINATES Continent derived from coordinates   Warning  assertions
## # ℹ 116 more rows
```

The easiest thing to do with these is simply download them with your chosen records, and 
do your own checking on the data. This can be achived via `select()`:


``` r
df <- galah_call() |>
  identify("Eolophus roseicapilla") |>
  filter(year >= 2020,
         basisOfRecord == "PRESERVED_SPECIMEN") |>
  select(group = c("basic", "assertions")) |>
  collect()
```

As you can see, there are a huge number of assertions, and they will take some processing.
It is also inefficient to download data we don't need, only to filter it later. Therefore,
it is worth considering filtering out some problematic records as part of our usual filtering
strategy.

### Data quality profiles

Data quality 'profiles' are pre-populated filter statements curated by the ALA that are 
designed to remove problematic records. They provide a quick and straightforward way to 
remove these records without having to construct elaborate filter statements.


``` r
show_all_profiles()
```

```
## # A tibble: 5 × 4
##      id short_name name                                  description                                                                                                                                             
##   <int> <chr>      <chr>                                 <chr>                                                                                                                                                   
## 1    92 ALA        ALA General                           "The default ALA profile filters out records based on the filter groups outlined below.  This is a moderately restricted set of data."                  
## 2   124 CSDM       Species Distribution Modelling (CSDM) "Base filters for the Collaborative Species Distribution Modelling program"                                                                             
## 3   133 re-usable  Data licensed for all uses            "Data licensed for re-use, including commercial uses. This profile only filters on license, no \"quality\" filters are applied."                        
## 4   224 AVH        AVH                                   "AVH data quality profile"                                                                                                                              
## 5   252 ALA-test   ALA General Test                      "A test version of the default ALA profile filters out records based on the filter groups outlined below.  This is a moderately restricted set of data."
```

Let's take a look at the most obvious one first:


``` r
search_all(profiles, "CSDM") |>
  show_values() |>
  gt::gt()
```


This is ok, but also needs unpacking. 

`spatiallyValid` is an amalgam of other assertions. At time of writing, `true` means that the 
latitude and longitude are known and within +/- 90 and 180 degrees (respectively), but are not 
0,0, and that there isn't a mismatch between the observed country and the country listed by 
the data provider. There are some minor other points, but that's about it.

Excluding potentially duplicate records is fairly clear and sensible, albeit also easily achieved
using thinning.

The remaining points are more contentious. The choice to include records since 1970 is clearly 
context-specific. More importantly, excluding points that are an outlier against any environmental
layer is a high penalty, particularly for rare species. This is likely to falsely exclude records
on a frequent basis.

Let's look at the 'ALA general' approach:


``` r
 search_all(profiles, "ALA") |>
  show_values() |>
  gt::gt()
```

There is a lot here and we won't go through it all; but two points are potentially useful.
First, this makes a lot of assumptions about what is and is not useful, with 26 separate
filters. This is a lot, and while most of them are useful in some contexts, equally this 
may be too stringent a set of tests for some applications. Applying it to our earlier example,
we see it only removes two records, but your milage will vary for different queries:


``` r
galah_call() |>
  identify("Eolophus roseicapilla") |>
  filter(year >= 2020,
         basisOfRecord == "PRESERVED_SPECIMEN") |>
  apply_profile("ALA") |>
  count() |>
  collect()
```

```
## # A tibble: 1 × 1
##   count
##   <int>
## 1    40
```

Second, the `filter` column lists how the query is sent to the ALA; this can be useful 
for replicating parts of the workflow that are useful for your specific application.
We'll try this out below.

### Bespoke filters using assertions

For example purposes, let's say we wanted to implement assertions based on the new
[TDWG Data Quality Standard](https://bdq.tdwg.org/draft/docs/list/bdquc/index.html#bdquc_SDM-Trees).
How would we do that?


### User assertions

An alternative approach is to call 'user assertions'; flags placed by users on individual 
suspect records. You can find records flagged in this way as follows:


``` r
galah_call() |>
  count(userAssertions) |>
  collect()
```

```
## # A tibble: 4 × 3
##   userAssertions_id userAssertions_label count
##   <chr>             <chr>                <int>
## 1 50005             Unconfirmed           9831
## 2 50003             Corrected             3489
## 3 50002             Verified               416
## 4 50001             Open issue              86
```

The categories here are a little obscure, but cross-referencing with the ALA data quality profile,
it appears that only issues that are 'Open' (code `50001`) or 'Unconfirmed' (code `50005`) have some
likelihood of being 'true' errors. Another point to consider is *who* is making these assertions:


``` r
galah_call() |>
  filter(userAssertions %in% c("50001", "50005")) |>
  count(assertionUserId) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  collect()
```

```
## Limiting to first 10 of 1,297 rows.
## Use `atlas_counts(limit = )` to return more rows.
```

```
## # A tibble: 10 × 3
##    assertionUserId_id assertionUserId_label count
##    <chr>              <chr>                 <int>
##  1 124186             Cameron Slatyer        1257
##  2 57159              Thomas Mesaglio        1232
##  3 2126               Niels Klazenga          932
##  4 3334               Penelope Mills          287
##  5 8902               ralph FOSTER            203
##  6 11936              Kay Durham              187
##  7 1108               Allen Sundholm          178
##  8 29516              Wendy Potts             165
##  9 25919              Matthew Connors         148
## 10 34050              Kimberi Pullen          141
```

This isn't actually terribly informative unless we know who these people are. But it likely
that the types of errors flagged by a single user will reflect their spatial and taxonomic
knowledge of the Australian biota.

To remove any records with user assertions, use `is.na(userAssertions)` within your filter 
statement:


``` r
galah_call() |>
  filter(is.na(userAssertions)) |>
  count() |>
  collect()
```

```
## # A tibble: 1 × 1
##       count
##       <int>
## 1 186070186
```

### Concluding remarks

Data quality is an ongoing topic of investigation for researchers and data infrastructures.
The tools described above are the current best available toolset implemented at the 
institutional level. For a more general assessment of how to handle data quality issues in 
R, see [Cleaning Biodiversity Data in R](https://cleaning-data-r.ala.org.au) by 
Dax Kellie et al. (2026, https://doi.org/10.54102/ala.77009).

A critical limitation of data quality assertions and their derivatives is that they focus 
exclusively on rule-based methods. There is no probabilistic element to them. Users seeking 
to draw probabilistic inference from these data will need to consider carefully whether there
are classes of outlier relevant to their use case, but utterly invisible to the systems in 
question.
